9.1 Comprehensive Healthcare Analytics Case
A healthcare system wants to evaluate whether a new patient education program improves medication adherence. They collected data from 60 patients in each group.

# Create the dataset
set.seed(505)
adherence_study <- tibble(
  group = rep(c("Control", "Education Program"), each = 60),
  adherence_score = c(
    rnorm(60, mean = 65, sd = 15),    # Control
    rnorm(60, mean = 72, sd = 14)     # Treatment
  ),
  age = c(
    rnorm(60, mean = 58, sd = 12),
    rnorm(60, mean = 59, sd = 11)
  )
)

# View summary
adherence_study %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    Mean = round(mean(adherence_score), 1),
    SD = round(sd(adherence_score), 1),
    Median = round(median(adherence_score), 1)
  ) %>%
  kable() %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))

9.1.1 Your Tasks:

Identify the measurement scale for adherence_score
Create a visualization comparing the two groups
Conduct a t-test to compare means
Calculate the effect size (Cohen’s d)
Write a conclusion for hospital leadership


# Your code here:

# 1. Visualization
ggplot(adherence_study, aes(x = group, y = adherence_score, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot() +

# 2. T-test

TipClick for Sample Analysis and Conclusion






# Full analysis
t_adherence <- t.test(adherence_score ~ group, data = adherence_study)
d_adherence <- cohens_d(adherence_score ~ group, data = adherence_study)

# Results
cat("T-test p-value:", round(t_adherence$p.value, 4), "\n")

T-test p-value: 0 

cat("Mean difference:", round(diff(t_adherence$estimate), 1), "points\n")

Mean difference: 12.1 points

cat("95% CI:", round(t_adherence$conf.int, 1), "\n")

95% CI: -17.4 -6.8

Cohen's d: -0.82 


Sample Conclusion for Leadership:

The patient education program showed a statistically significant improvement in medication adherence scores compared to standard care (p = 0). Patients in the education program scored an average of 12.1 points higher (95% CI: 6.8 to 17.4 points).
The effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.82) suggests a medium practical effect. Given that improved medication adherence is associated with reduced hospital readmissions and better health outcomes, we recommend implementing this education program system-wide.

title: Week 3: Basic Statistical Concepts
text:
10.1 Module Summary

Measurement scales determine which statistics are appropriate

Nominal → Mode, Frequencies
Ordinal → Mode, Median, Range
Interval/Ratio → Mean, SD

Central tendency describes the typical value; dispersion describes spread
Distribution shape affects choice of central tendency measure

Skewed data → Median often better than Mean

Hypothesis testing helps us make inferences about populations from samples

p-value = probability of data under H₀, NOT probability that H₀ is true

Effect size and confidence intervals are essential complements to p-values
Statistical significance ≠ Practical importance

title: Week 02: A Primer on R, RStudio, Quarto, and Data Wrangling
text:
R is a programming language and software environment specifically designed for statistical computing and data analysis. Originally developed in the early 1990s by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman at the University of Auckland, New Zealand, R has become one of the most widely used tools for data science and analytics.


R offers several compelling advantages for healthcare management professionals:

Free and Open Source: Unlike expensive proprietary software (SAS, SPSS), R is completely free
Extensive Healthcare Packages: Specialized packages for survival analysis, epidemiology, clinical trials, and health economics
Reproducibility: Create documented, reproducible analyses essential for regulatory compliance and research
Visualization: Create publication-quality graphs and interactive dashboards
Community Support: Large community of healthcare data scientists sharing code and solutions
Industry Adoption: Increasingly used by hospitals, pharmaceutical companies, insurance providers, and public health organizations




According to various surveys and rankings:

Consistently ranked in the top 10 programming languages for data science
Over 20,000 packages available on CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network)
Widely used in academic research, with thousands of peer-reviewed papers using R
Growing adoption in healthcare industry for predictive analytics, outcomes research, and quality improvement





RStudio is an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) for R. Think of it as a user-friendly workspace that makes working with R much easier and more efficient.
Analogy: If R is the engine of a car, RStudio is the dashboard, steering wheel, and all the controls that help you drive effectively.



Organized workspace with multiple panes
Code completion and syntax highlighting
Easy package management
Integrated help and documentation
Version control integration (Git)
Direct creation of reports and presentations (via Quarto/R Markdown)








Go to https://cran.r-project.org/
Click on your operating system (Windows, Mac, or Linux)
Download and run the installer
Follow the installation prompts (default settings are fine)





Go to https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/
Download RStudio Desktop (Free version)
Run the installer
Follow the installation prompts







Important



Important: Always install R first, then RStudio. RStudio needs R to function.

text:
2.1 The Four Panes

2.1.1 1. Source Pane (Top-Left)

Where you write and edit your R scripts and Quarto documents
Code here is NOT executed until you run it
Save your work here for future use
Think of it as your “notepad” for code



2.1.2 2. Console Pane (Bottom-Left)

Where R actually executes commands
Shows output and results
Can type commands directly here (but they won’t be saved)
Displays error messages and warnings



2.1.3 3. Environment/History Pane (Top-Right)

Environment tab: Shows all objects (data, variables) currently in memory
History tab: Record of all commands you’ve run
Connections tab: Database connections
Think of Environment as your “workspace inventory”



2.1.4 4. Files/Plots/Packages/Help Pane (Bottom-Right)

Files: Navigate your computer’s file system
Plots: Displays graphs and visualizations
Packages: Install and manage R packages
Help: Access documentation and help files
Viewer: Preview HTML content and Quarto documents

title: Week 02: A Primer on R, RStudio, Quarto, and Data Wrangling
text:
3.1 What is Quarto?
Quarto is an open-source scientific and technical publishing system that allows you to combine:

Code (R, Python, and other languages)
Text (formatted with Markdown)
Output (tables, figures, results)

…all in a single document that can be rendered to multiple formats (HTML, PDF, Word, presentations).

3.1.1 Why Use Quarto?

Reproducibility: Your analysis and documentation are in one place
Professional Reports: Create polished reports directly from your analysis
Multiple Formats: One source document → many output formats
Version Control Friendly: Plain text files work well with Git
Collaboration: Easy to share and review



3.1.2 Quarto vs R Markdown
Quarto is the next-generation version of R Markdown. If you’ve heard of R Markdown, Quarto offers:

Better support for multiple programming languages
Improved features for books, websites, and presentations
More consistent syntax across output formats

title: Week 02: A Primer on R, RStudio, Quarto, and Data Wrangling
text:
3.2 Basic Quarto Document Structure
A Quarto document (.qmd file) has three main parts:

3.2.1 1. YAML Header
---
title: "My Analysis"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format: html
---
This controls document metadata and output settings.


3.2.2 2. Markdown Text
Regular text with formatting:
# Heading 1
## Heading 2

**Bold text** and *italic text*

- Bullet point 1
- Bullet point 2

1. Numbered item 1
2. Numbered item 2


3.2.3 3. Code Chunks
R code is placed in special “chunks”:

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Your R code here
mean(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3
```


:::
:::


3.2.4 Rendering Your Document

Click the Render button in RStudio, or
Use keyboard shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+K (Windows) or Cmd+Shift+K (Mac)







NoteExercise 1: Create Your First Quarto Document




In RStudio, go to File → New File → Quarto Document
Give it a title “My First Analysis”
Keep HTML as the format
Click “Create”
Click “Render” to see the output

4.1 Your First R Commands
Let’s start with some simple operations in R. You can type these directly in the Console or in a code chunk.

4.1.1 Basic Arithmetic

# Addition
5 + 3

[1] 8

# Subtraction

[1] 6

# Multiplication

[1] 42

# Division
20 / 4

[1] 5

# Exponentiation (power)
2^3

[1] 8

# Modulo (remainder)

[1] 2




4.1.2 Creating Variables
Variables store values for later use. Use the assignment operator <- (or =).

# Assign values to variables
patient_count <- 150
average_los <- 4.5  # LOS = Length of Stay

# View the values
patient_count

[1] 150

average_los

[1] 4.5

# Use variables in calculations
total_patient_days <- patient_count * average_los
total_patient_days

[1] 675








Tip



Naming Conventions: Use descriptive names with underscores (snake_case) or periods. Avoid spaces and special characters. Names are case-sensitive (Age ≠ age).




4.1.3 Comments
Use # to add comments—text that R ignores but helps humans understand the code.

# This is a comment - R ignores this line

7.1 What are Packages?
Packages are collections of R functions, data, and documentation that extend R’s capabilities. Think of them as “apps” for R.

7.1.1 Installing Packages
You only need to install a package once (like downloading an app).

# Install a single package
install.packages("tidyverse")

# Install multiple packages
install.packages(c("readxl", "janitor", "lubridate"))



7.1.2 Loading Packages
You need to load a package each time you start R (like opening an app).

# Load a package
library(tidyverse)

title: Week 02: A Primer on R, RStudio, Quarto, and Data Wrangling
text:
7.2 Introduction to the Tidyverse
The tidyverse is a collection of R packages designed for data science. They share a common philosophy and grammar, making them easy to learn and use together.

# Load the tidyverse
library(tidyverse)


7.2.1 Core Tidyverse Packages



Package
Purpose




dplyr
Data manipulation (filter, select, mutate, summarize)


ggplot2
Data visualization


tidyr
Data tidying (reshape data)


readr
Reading rectangular data (CSV, TSV)


tibble
Modern data frames


stringr
String manipulation


forcats
Working with factors


purrr
Functional programming





7.2.2 The Tidyverse Philosophy

Tidy data: Each variable is a column, each observation is a row
Consistent syntax: Functions work similarly across packages
Pipe-friendly: Chain operations together with |> or %>%
Human-readable: Code reads almost like English

title: Week 02: A Primer on R, RStudio, Quarto, and Data Wrangling
text:
8.1 The Pipe Operator
Before we dive in, let’s learn the pipe operator |> (or %>%). It takes the output of one function and passes it as the first argument to the next function.

# Without pipe - nested functions (hard to read)
round(mean(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)), 2)

[1] 3

# With pipe - sequential operations (easy to read)
c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5) |>
  mean() |>
  round(2)

[1] 3


Read it as “and then”: Take this data, and then do this, and then do that.

text:
12.3 Step 2: Data Cleaning and Preparation

# Clean and prepare the data
clean_data <- healthcare_data |>
  mutate(
    # Create age groups
    age_group = case_when(
      age < 40 ~ "Under 40",
      age < 65 ~ "40-64",
      TRUE ~ "65+"
    ),
    # Create cost categories
    cost_category = case_when(
      total_charges < 5000 ~ "Low",
      total_charges < 20000 ~ "Medium",
      TRUE ~ "High"
    ),
    # Calculate cost per day
    cost_per_day = round(total_charges / los, 2)
  ) |>
  # Convert to factors with proper ordering
  mutate(
    age_group = factor(age_group, levels = c("Under 40", "40-64", "65+")),
    cost_category = factor(cost_category, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))
  )

title: Tree-Based Models in Healthcare Analytics
text:
In healthcare analytics, we often face prediction problems where the relationships between patient characteristics and outcomes are complex and non-linear. Consider these real-world scenarios that healthcare managers encounter daily:

Predicting healthcare costs: A patient’s annual healthcare expenditure depends on age, chronic conditions, prior utilization, and many other factors. These relationships are rarely simple linear associations—a 70-year-old diabetic patient with heart disease doesn’t simply cost “the sum” of these individual risk factors.
Estimating length of stay: Hospital administrators need accurate predictions for bed management and staffing. A patient’s expected length of stay depends on diagnosis, comorbidities, surgical procedures, and complications, often in complex, interacting ways.
Forecasting resource utilization: Health systems must anticipate demand for services. Utilization patterns vary dramatically across patient subgroups defined by combinations of clinical and demographic characteristics.

Traditional linear regression assumes that each predictor contributes additively to the outcome, with a constant effect across all patients. But in healthcare, this assumption often fails dramatically. For example, the effect of diabetes on healthcare costs might be minimal for young, otherwise healthy patients but substantial for elderly patients with multiple comorbidities. Tree-based models excel at capturing these kinds of complex interactions automatically, without requiring the analyst to specify them in advance.



The fundamental idea behind tree-based prediction is elegantly simple: divide patients into groups with similar outcomes, then predict the average outcome for each group. This process of recursive partitioning creates a hierarchical structure that resembles an inverted tree, with the root at the top containing all patients and branches leading down to “leaves” (terminal nodes) containing homogeneous subgroups.
Consider predicting annual healthcare costs. A tree algorithm might first split patients into those with prior-year costs above versus below $10,000. Among high-cost patients, it might further split by age (over 65 vs. under 65). Among low-cost patients, it might split by presence of chronic conditions. This continues until we have groups that are relatively homogeneous in their healthcare costs.
The beauty of this approach is that:

Interactions are automatic: If diabetes only matters for elderly patients, the tree will naturally split by age first, then by diabetes only in the elderly branch.
Non-linearities are handled: The tree doesn’t assume that the effect of age is linear—it can create different predictions for ages 20-40, 40-60, and 60-80 if that’s what the data support.
Results are interpretable: A tree can be visualized and explained to non-technical stakeholders. “Patients over 65 with prior hospitalization and diabetes are predicted to cost $45,000” is much more accessible than a regression equation.
No variable scaling needed: Unlike penalized regression, trees are invariant to monotonic transformations of predictors—you don’t need to worry about standardization.




Last week, we learned about penalized regression methods (Ridge, LASSO, Elastic Net) for prediction. This week, we explore an entirely different approach to the same fundamental problem: predicting outcomes from patient characteristics while avoiding overfitting.
Both approaches share common principles:

Training vs. test data: We evaluate predictive performance on data not used to build the model
Cross-validation: We use CV to select tuning parameters that balance bias and variance
Regularization: We control model complexity to prevent overfitting

However, the methods differ fundamentally in how they model the relationship between predictors and outcome:



Aspect
Penalized Regression
Tree-Based Models




Functional form
Linear combinations
Piecewise constant


Interactions
Must be specified
Automatic


Interpretability
Coefficients
Visual tree structure


Feature selection
Via shrinkage (LASSO)
Via split selection


Prediction surface
Smooth
Step function



By the end of this module, you’ll understand when each approach is most appropriate and how to compare their performance for healthcare prediction problems.



By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Explain the recursive partitioning algorithm that underlies regression trees, including how splits are chosen and when to stop growing
Interpret tree diagrams and translate them into actionable predictions and business rules for healthcare applications
Understand the bias-variance tradeoff in tree complexity and how pruning addresses overfitting
Implement regression trees in R using the rpart package, including hyperparameter tuning via cross-validation
Compare tree-based predictions with linear regression and penalized regression on healthcare data
Explain the motivation for ensemble methods like bagging and random forests that address the high variance of individual trees
Apply random forests using the randomForest or ranger packages and interpret variable importance measures
Evaluate and compare model performance using appropriate metrics for continuous outcomes (RMSE, MAE, R²)

title: Tree-Based Models in Healthcare Analytics
section: 2.1 How Trees Make Predictions: The Big Picture
text:
2.1 How Trees Make Predictions: The Big Picture
Before diving into the algorithmic details, let’s understand the conceptual framework. A regression tree predicts a continuous outcome (like healthcare costs) by:

Partitioning the predictor space into rectangular regions
Assigning a predicted value to each region (the average outcome of training observations in that region)

For a new patient, we simply determine which region their predictor values fall into and predict the corresponding average. This is fundamentally different from regression, which computes a weighted sum of predictor values.

2.1.1 Visual Intuition
Imagine predicting healthcare costs based on just two variables: age and number of chronic conditions. A regression tree might create predictions like this:

Region 1: Age < 50 AND Conditions < 2 → Predict $3,000
Region 2: Age < 50 AND Conditions ≥ 2 → Predict $8,500
Region 3: Age ≥ 50 AND Conditions < 3 → Predict $12,000
Region 4: Age ≥ 50 AND Conditions ≥ 3 → Predict $35,000

Notice how the tree captures an interaction: for younger patients, having 2+ conditions increases predicted costs from $3,000 to $8,500 (a 2.8x increase). For older patients, going from <3 to ≥3 conditions increases predicted costs from $12,000 to $35,000 (a 2.9x increase). The tree automatically discovered that the “cost impact” of chronic conditions varies by age group.

title: Tree-Based Models in Healthcare Analytics
text:
2.2 The Recursive Partitioning Algorithm
Now let’s understand how the algorithm constructs these partitions. The process is called “recursive binary splitting” because at each step, we:

Consider all possible ways to split the current region into two parts
Choose the split that most improves our predictions
Recursively apply the same process to each resulting region


2.2.1 Step 1: Finding the Best Split
At each node, we need to decide: - Which variable to split on - What value to use as the cutoff
For a regression tree predicting a continuous outcome Y, the algorithm evaluates every possible split by computing the reduction in sum of squared errors (SSE).
Suppose we’re considering splitting predictor X at value c, creating two groups:

Left group (R₁): Observations where X < c
Right group (R₂): Observations where X ≥ c

For each group, the predicted value is simply the mean of Y for observations in that group:
\[\hat{y}_{R_1} = \frac{1}{n_1} \sum_{i: x_i < c} y_i \quad \text{and} \quad \hat{y}_{R_2} = \frac{1}{n_2} \sum_{i: x_i \geq c} y_i\]
The SSE for this split is:
\[\text{SSE}(X, c) = \sum_{i: x_i < c} (y_i - \hat{y}_{R_1})^2 + \sum_{i: x_i \geq c} (y_i - \hat{y}_{R_2})^2\]
The algorithm tries every variable and every possible cutoff value, selecting the combination (X, c) that minimizes SSE. This is a “greedy” approach—we make the locally optimal choice at each step without considering whether a different choice might lead to a better tree overall.


2.2.2 Step 2: Recursive Splitting
Once we’ve made the first split, we have two regions. We now apply the exact same process to each region independently:

Among observations in the left region, find the best split
Among observations in the right region, find the best split
Continue recursively on each resulting region

This process creates a tree structure where each internal node represents a split decision and each terminal node (leaf) represents a prediction.


2.2.3 Step 3: Stopping Criteria
The algorithm must know when to stop splitting. Common stopping criteria include:

Minimum node size: Don’t split nodes with fewer than some threshold of observations (e.g., 20)
Maximum depth: Limit the number of levels in the tree
Minimum improvement: Stop if no split improves SSE by more than a threshold

However, these early stopping rules are often too aggressive—they might prevent a “good” split that would occur later. Instead, modern implementations typically grow a large tree and then prune it back.

title: Tree-Based Models in Healthcare Analytics
section: 2.3 Overfitting and the Need for Pruning
text:
2.3 Overfitting and the Need for Pruning

2.3.1 The Problem: Trees Can Perfectly Fit Training Data
If we let a tree grow without restriction, it will continue splitting until each terminal node contains very few observations (perhaps even just one). Such a tree will have:

Zero training error: Each prediction equals the actual outcome
Poor test performance: The tree has memorized the training data, including its random noise

This is overfitting in its purest form. The tree is too complex—it has high variance (predictions change dramatically with different training samples) even though it has low bias (it can approximate any pattern).


2.3.2 Visual Illustration of Overfitting
Consider predicting healthcare costs from age alone. Imagine we have 100 patients:

A 1-split tree might divide patients into age < 50 vs. ≥ 50, giving 2 predictions
A 10-split tree creates 11 predictions, each based on roughly 9 patients
A 99-split tree creates 100 predictions, each based on 1 patient

The 99-split tree fits the training data perfectly but will perform terribly on new data because each prediction is based on a single patient’s random cost variation.


2.3.3 The Solution: Cost-Complexity Pruning
Rather than deciding when to stop growing, we grow a large tree and then prune branches that don’t improve test performance enough to justify their complexity. This is done by minimizing a penalized error criterion:
\[\text{Cost-Complexity} = \text{SSE} + \alpha \cdot |T|\]
Where: - SSE is the sum of squared errors on the training data - |T| is the number of terminal nodes in the tree - α (alpha) is a complexity parameter that controls the tradeoff
This should look familiar from last week! Just as LASSO penalizes regression coefficients to achieve a simpler model, cost-complexity pruning penalizes tree size. The parameter α plays the same role as λ in penalized regression:

α = 0: No penalty → full tree (overfitting)
α large: Heavy penalty → small tree (underfitting)

We use cross-validation to find the optimal α that minimizes prediction error.


2.3.4 The 1-SE Rule
When selecting α via cross-validation, we often use the “one standard error rule”:

Compute the cross-validated error for each value of α
Find α* that minimizes CV error
Select the largest α (simplest tree) whose CV error is within one standard error of the minimum

This rule trades a tiny bit of predictive accuracy for a substantially simpler, more interpretable tree. In practice, the simpler tree often performs just as well on truly new data.

title: Tree-Based Models in Healthcare Analytics
text:
2.4 Advantages and Limitations of Trees

2.4.1 Advantages

Interpretability: Trees can be visualized and explained to non-technical stakeholders. You can literally trace the path from root to leaf and understand why a prediction was made.
No preprocessing required: Trees handle numeric and categorical predictors naturally, don’t require scaling/standardization, and are invariant to monotonic transformations.
Automatic interaction detection: If diabetes only matters for elderly patients, the tree will discover this automatically.
Handle missing data: Trees can use “surrogate splits” to make predictions when some values are missing.
Computationally efficient: Predictions are extremely fast—just a series of if-then comparisons.



2.4.2 Limitations

High variance: Small changes in the training data can lead to very different trees. This instability is the primary motivation for ensemble methods.
Piecewise constant predictions: Trees approximate smooth relationships with step functions, which can be inefficient when the true relationship is smooth.
Greedy algorithm: The recursive splitting may miss globally optimal solutions because it doesn’t look ahead.
Extrapolation issues: Trees cannot extrapolate beyond the range of training data—they simply predict the average of the nearest terminal node.
Not ideal for additive relationships: If the true model is Y = β₁X₁ + β₂X₂ (purely additive), a tree needs many splits to approximate this, while linear regression captures it exactly.

title: Tree-Based Models in Healthcare Analytics
section: 3.2 Creating a Healthcare Cost Prediction Dataset
text:
3.2 Creating a Healthcare Cost Prediction Dataset
For this tutorial, we’ll create a realistic simulated dataset representing patients in a healthcare system. Our goal is to predict annual healthcare costs based on patient characteristics, health conditions, and prior utilization. This mirrors the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) data that you’ll use for the assignment.

3.2.1 The Data Generation Process
We’ll simulate data that captures several realistic features of healthcare cost prediction:

Non-linear age effects: Healthcare costs don’t increase linearly with age—they rise more steeply after 60
Interactions: The effect of chronic conditions depends on age
Heavy-tailed costs: Healthcare spending has many low-cost patients and some very high-cost outliers
Multiple predictor types: Both continuous (age, BMI) and categorical (insurance, region) variables

Let’s create this dataset:


Show code
# Create simulated healthcare cost dataset
n <- 1000  # Number of patients

# Generate patient characteristics
healthcare_data <- data.frame(
  # Demographics
  age = round(runif(n, 18, 85)),
  sex = sample(c("Male", "Female"), n, replace = TRUE),

  # Health behaviors and conditions
  bmi = round(rnorm(n, 28, 6), 1),
  smoker = sample(c(0, 1), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.8, 0.2)),

  # Chronic conditions (more likely with age)
  diabetes = NA,
  hypertension = NA,
  heart_disease = NA,

  # Healthcare access
  insurance = sample(c("Private", "Medicare", "Medicaid", "Uninsured"),
                     n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.1)),

  # Prior utilization
  prior_er_visits = rpois(n, lambda = 0.5),
  prior_hospitalizations = rpois(n, lambda = 0.15),

  # Geography
  region = sample(c("Northeast", "Midwest", "South", "West"),
                  n, replace = TRUE)
)

# Generate chronic conditions with age-dependent probabilities
# This creates realistic correlations between age and chronic conditions
healthcare_data <- healthcare_data %>%
  mutate(
    # Diabetes more likely with age and high BMI
    diabetes = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-3 + 0.03 * age + 0.05 * bmi)),

    # Hypertension more likely with age
    hypertension = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-2 + 0.04 * age)),

    # Heart disease more likely with age, smoking, and other conditions
    heart_disease = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-4 + 0.05 * age + 0.5 * smoker +
                                         0.3 * diabetes + 0.3 * hypertension)),

    # Count of chronic conditions
    n_conditions = diabetes + hypertension + heart_disease
  )

# Generate healthcare costs with realistic complexity
# This is the "true" relationship that our models will try to discover
healthcare_data <- healthcare_data %>%
  mutate(
    # Base cost depends on age (non-linear)
    base_cost = 1000 + 50 * age + 0.5 * age^2,

    # Condition costs (with interactions!)
    condition_cost = 3000 * diabetes + 2500 * hypertension +
                     5000 * heart_disease +
                     # Interaction: conditions cost more for older patients
                     50 * age * n_conditions,

    # Utilization-driven costs
    utilization_cost = 2000 * prior_er_visits +
                       15000 * prior_hospitalizations,

    # Behavior costs
    behavior_cost = 1500 * smoker + 50 * pmax(bmi - 30, 0),

    # Insurance effects (uninsured have lower recorded costs due to less care)
    insurance_effect = case_when(
      insurance == "Private" ~ 1.0,
      insurance == "Medicare" ~ 1.1,  # Higher utilization
      insurance == "Medicaid" ~ 0.9,
      insurance == "Uninsured" ~ 0.6
    ),

    # Combine all components
    expected_cost = (base_cost + condition_cost + utilization_cost +
                     behavior_cost) * insurance_effect,

    # Add realistic noise (log-normal to create heavy tail)
    annual_cost = round(expected_cost * exp(rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)))
  ) %>%
  # Clean up intermediate variables
  select(-base_cost, -condition_cost, -utilization_cost,
         -behavior_cost, -insurance_effect, -expected_cost)

# Convert categorical variables to factors
healthcare_data <- healthcare_data %>%
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex),
    insurance = factor(insurance),
    region = factor(region),
    smoker = factor(smoker, labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    diabetes = factor(diabetes, labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    hypertension = factor(hypertension, labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    heart_disease = factor(heart_disease, labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  )

# Display dataset structure
cat("Dataset Overview:\n")

3.2.3 Key Observations
Looking at our exploratory analysis, we can note several important features:

Right-skewed costs: The distribution of healthcare costs is heavily right-skewed, with many low-cost patients and a long tail of high-cost patients. This is typical of healthcare spending data.
Non-linear age relationship: The relationship between age and costs is not linear—costs increase more steeply at older ages. Trees should capture this automatically.
Strong condition effects: The number of chronic conditions is strongly associated with costs. We built in interactions with age that trees should discover.
Heterogeneous patient population: Our data includes a mix of young healthy patients (low cost) and older patients with multiple conditions (high cost).

3.4.2 The Complexity Parameter (cp)
The complexity parameter cp is the most important tuning parameter. It controls the cost-complexity pruning discussed earlier:

A split is only performed if it improves the model by at least cp * (SSE of root node)
Higher cp → fewer splits → simpler trees
Lower cp → more splits → complex trees

Let’s see how cp affects tree size:


Show code
# Fit trees with different cp values
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

cp_values <- c(0.1, 0.03, 0.01, 0.001)

for (cp_val in cp_values) {
  tree_temp <- rpart(
    annual_cost ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + diabetes +
                  hypertension + heart_disease + insurance +
                  prior_er_visits + prior_hospitalizations + region,
    data = healthcare_data,
    method = "anova",
    control = rpart.control(cp = cp_val)
  )

  # Count terminal nodes
  n_leaves <- sum(tree_temp$frame$var == "<leaf>")

  rpart.plot(tree_temp,
             main = paste0("cp = ", cp_val, " (", n_leaves, " leaves)"),
             cex = 0.6)
}

text:
3.5 Evaluating Model Performance

3.5.1 Train-Test Split Approach
For a fair evaluation, we should test our model on data it hasn’t seen. Let’s split our data and evaluate performance properly:


Show code
# Create train-test split (70-30)
set.seed(123)
train_idx <- sample(1:nrow(healthcare_data), 0.7 * nrow(healthcare_data))
train_data <- healthcare_data[train_idx, ]
test_data <- healthcare_data[-train_idx, ]

cat("Data Split:\n")


Data Split:


Show code
cat("===========\n")


===========


Show code
cat("Training set:", nrow(train_data), "patients\n")


Training set: 700 patients


Show code
cat("Test set:", nrow(test_data), "patients\n")


Test set: 300 patients




3.5.2 Building and Evaluating the Tree


Show code
# Fit tree on training data
tree_train <- rpart(
  annual_cost ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + diabetes +
                hypertension + heart_disease + insurance +
                prior_er_visits + prior_hospitalizations + region,
  data = train_data,
  method = "anova",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.001)
)

# Prune using 1-SE rule
best_cp <- tree_train$cptable[which.min(tree_train$cptable[,"xerror"]), "CP"]
tree_final <- prune(tree_train, cp = best_cp)

# Make predictions on test set
predictions <- predict(tree_final, test_data)

# Calculate performance metrics
actual <- test_data$annual_cost

# Root Mean Squared Error
rmse <- sqrt(mean((actual - predictions)^2))

# Mean Absolute Error
mae <- mean(abs(actual - predictions))

# R-squared
ss_res <- sum((actual - predictions)^2)
ss_tot <- sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
r_squared <- 1 - (ss_res / ss_tot)

# Mean Absolute Percentage Error
mape <- mean(abs((actual - predictions) / actual)) * 100

cat("Test Set Performance:\n")

Show code

R-squared: 0.551 


Show code
cat("MAPE:", round(mape, 1), "%\n")


MAPE: 38.5 %




3.5.3 Visualizing Predictions vs. Actual
Let’s see how well our predictions match actual costs:


Show code
# Create prediction comparison plot
pred_df <- data.frame(
  Actual = actual,
  Predicted = predictions
)

ggplot(pred_df, aes(x = Actual/1000, y = Predicted/1000)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Regression Tree: Predicted vs. Actual Healthcare Costs",
    x = "Actual Cost ($1000s)",
    y = "Predicted Cost ($1000s)"
  ) +

Interpretation: Points along the red dashed line represent perfect predictions. The horizontal bands in predictions occur because the tree only produces a discrete number of predicted values (one per leaf node). This is a characteristic of tree-based predictions—they’re piecewise constant.

section: 3.6 Comparing with Linear and Penalized Regression
text:
3.6 Comparing with Linear and Penalized Regression
Now let’s compare our tree model with the regression methods from previous weeks. This comparison will help you understand when each approach is most appropriate.


Show code
# 1. Linear Regression
lm_model <- lm(
  annual_cost ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + diabetes +
                hypertension + heart_disease + insurance +
                prior_er_visits + prior_hospitalizations + region,
  data = train_data
)

# 2. Penalized Regression (LASSO)
# Prepare matrices for glmnet
x_train <- model.matrix(
  ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + diabetes + hypertension +
    heart_disease + insurance + prior_er_visits +
    prior_hospitalizations + region - 1,
  data = train_data
)
y_train <- train_data$annual_cost

x_test <- model.matrix(
  ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + diabetes + hypertension +
    heart_disease + insurance + prior_er_visits +
    prior_hospitalizations + region - 1,
  data = test_data
)

# Fit LASSO with cross-validation
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 1)

# 3. Ridge Regression
ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 0)

# Make predictions
pred_lm <- predict(lm_model, test_data)
pred_lasso <- predict(lasso_cv, x_test, s = "lambda.1se")
pred_ridge <- predict(ridge_cv, x_test, s = "lambda.1se")
pred_tree <- predict(tree_final, test_data)

# Calculate RMSE for each model
rmse_lm <- sqrt(mean((actual - pred_lm)^2))
rmse_lasso <- sqrt(mean((actual - pred_lasso)^2))
rmse_ridge <- sqrt(mean((actual - pred_ridge)^2))
rmse_tree <- sqrt(mean((actual - pred_tree)^2))

# Calculate R-squared for each
r2_lm <- 1 - sum((actual - pred_lm)^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
r2_lasso <- 1 - sum((actual - pred_lasso)^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
r2_ridge <- 1 - sum((actual - pred_ridge)^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
r2_tree <- 1 - sum((actual - pred_tree)^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)

# Create comparison table
comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Linear Regression", "Ridge Regression", "LASSO", "Regression Tree"),
  RMSE = c(rmse_lm, rmse_ridge, rmse_lasso, rmse_tree),
  R_squared = c(r2_lm, r2_ridge, r2_lasso, r2_tree)
)

comparison <- comparison %>%
  mutate(
    RMSE = round(RMSE, 0),
    R_squared = round(R_squared, 3)
  ) %>%
  arrange(RMSE)

cat("Model Comparison on Test Set:\n")


Model Comparison on Test Set:


Show code
cat("=============================\n\n")


=============================


Show code
print(comparison, row.names = FALSE)


             Model RMSE R_squared
             LASSO 6568     0.679
 Linear Regression 6674     0.668
  Ridge Regression 6756     0.660
   Regression Tree 7763     0.551



3.6.1 Visualizing Model Comparison


Show code
# Create comparison visualization
comparison_long <- comparison %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(RMSE, R_squared),
               names_to = "Metric",
               values_to = "Value")

ggplot(comparison, aes(x = reorder(Model, -RMSE), y = RMSE, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("$", format(RMSE, big.mark = ","))),
            vjust = -0.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Model Comparison: Test Set RMSE",
    x = "",
    y = "Root Mean Squared Error ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1))











3.6.2 Discussion of Results
The comparison reveals important insights about these different modeling approaches:

Regression Tree Performance: Trees automatically capture non-linear relationships and interactions that we built into the data, potentially outperforming linear models that assume additivity.
Linear vs. Penalized Regression: Ridge and LASSO may perform similarly to linear regression if there’s no need for variable selection or coefficient shrinkage.
Trade-offs: Trees sacrifice smooth predictions for the ability to capture complex interactions. The “stepped” nature of tree predictions may be less accurate for truly smooth relationships.

title: Tree-Based Models in Healthcare Analytics
text:
4.1 The Problem with Single Trees
While regression trees are interpretable and capture complex relationships, they suffer from a critical problem: high variance. This means that small changes in the training data can lead to very different trees, making predictions unstable.

4.1.1 Demonstrating Tree Instability
Let’s see this instability in action by fitting trees to different bootstrap samples of our data:


Show code
# Fit trees to 4 different bootstrap samples
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

for (i in 1:4) {
  # Create bootstrap sample
  boot_idx <- sample(1:nrow(healthcare_data), replace = TRUE)
  boot_data <- healthcare_data[boot_idx, ]

  # Fit tree
  boot_tree <- rpart(
    annual_cost ~ age + sex + bmi + smoker + diabetes +
                  hypertension + heart_disease + insurance +
                  prior_er_visits + prior_hospitalizations,
    data = boot_data,
    method = "anova",
    control = rpart.control(cp = 0.02)
  )

  # Plot
  rpart.plot(boot_tree, main = paste("Bootstrap Sample", i), cex = 0.6)
}

Observation: Notice how different the trees are! The same variables appear in different positions, different cutoff values are used, and different variables are selected. This instability is problematic because we don’t know which tree structure is “correct.”

title: Tree-Based Models in Healthcare Analytics
text:
4.2 The Random Forest Solution
Random forests address tree instability through two key ideas:

4.2.1 1. Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating)
Instead of building one tree, we build many trees on different bootstrap samples and average their predictions:

Draw B bootstrap samples from the training data
Fit a tree to each sample
For prediction, average across all B trees

This reduces variance because the averaging smooths out the individual trees’ errors. If each tree has variance σ², and the trees are independent, the ensemble has variance σ²/B.


4.2.2 2. Random Feature Selection
Bagging alone isn’t enough—the trees are too correlated because they all use the same best predictors at the top. Random forests add another layer of randomness:

At each split, only consider a random subset of m predictors (not all p)
This decorrelates the trees, making the averaging more effective
Default: m = p/3 for regression, m = √p for classification

4.4.1 Interpreting Variable Importance
%IncMSE (Permutation Importance):
For each tree, we predict the OOB samples and record the MSE. Then we randomly shuffle one variable and predict again. The increase in MSE reflects how important that variable is. Variables that cause large increases when shuffled are important.
IncNodePurity (Impurity Importance):
Sum of the reduction in squared error whenever the variable is used for a split, averaged over all trees.
Healthcare Interpretation:
The variable importance plot tells us which patient characteristics are most predictive of healthcare costs. For healthcare managers, this information can guide:

Care management targeting
Quality improvement initiatives

title: Tree-Based Models in Healthcare Analytics
text:
5.1 Conceptual Questions
Test your understanding of tree-based models with these questions:

5.1.1 Question 1: Algorithm Understanding
A regression tree is being built to predict hospital length of stay. The algorithm is considering splitting patients by age at cutoff 65. There are 200 patients younger than 65 with mean LOS = 3.2 days, and 100 patients 65+ with mean LOS = 5.8 days.

What would be the prediction for a 70-year-old patient after this split?
If the overall mean LOS before the split is 4.07 days, calculate the reduction in SSE from this split.
Why is finding the optimal split computationally intensive with continuous predictors?







TipClick for Answers






5.8 days - The prediction for any patient in a terminal node is the mean outcome of training observations in that node. A 70-year-old falls in the 65+ node with mean LOS = 5.8.
Reduction in SSE:

Before split: SSE = Σ(yᵢ - 4.07)² for all 300 patients
After split: SSE = Σ(yᵢ - 3.2)² for 200 young + Σ(yᵢ - 5.8)² for 100 old
The reduction = SSE_before - SSE_after
While we can’t compute exact values without individual data, the intuition is that predictions are now closer to actual values because we’ve separated two groups with different means.

For a continuous predictor with n unique values, there are (n-1) possible cutoff points to evaluate. For each cutoff, we must compute the SSE for both resulting groups. With many predictors and many observations, this requires checking thousands of potential splits at each node.






5.1.2 Question 2: Overfitting and Pruning
Explain why a regression tree with 100 terminal nodes fit to 100 training observations would be useless for prediction, even though its training MSE is zero.






TipClick for Answer





This tree has perfectly memorized the training data—each terminal node contains exactly one observation, so the prediction equals the actual value and training MSE is zero.
However, the predictions reflect individual patient variation, not true underlying patterns. When applied to new patients, the tree will:

Assign them to a terminal node based on the path they follow
Predict the single training observation’s outcome in that node
This prediction is essentially random from the new patient’s perspective

This is extreme overfitting. The model has high variance (predictions would change completely with different training data) and will perform poorly on test data. Pruning reduces the tree to capture genuine patterns rather than noise.





5.1.3 Question 3: Method Comparison
For each scenario, explain which method (linear regression, LASSO, regression tree, or random forest) would be most appropriate:

Predicting healthcare costs for a health plan with 500 members using 10 predictors. Interpretability is essential for explaining to executives.
Building a real-time risk scoring system for an EHR that must predict patient deterioration using 200+ clinical variables.
Analyzing the relationship between hospital characteristics and readmission rates for a policy study.







TipClick for Answers






Regression Tree - With only 500 observations and the need for interpretability, a pruned regression tree provides an easy-to-explain model. Random forest would give better predictions but can’t be visualized. LASSO could work but produces coefficient-based explanations that may be harder for executives.
Random Forest - With 200+ variables and real-time prediction needs, random forest handles many predictors well, automatically selects important variables, doesn’t need preprocessing, and predictions are fast once trained. The lack of interpretability matters less in automated systems.
Linear Regression or LASSO - For policy studies, we need valid statistical inference with confidence intervals and p-values. Tree methods don’t provide these. If variable selection is important, use LASSO to identify key hospital characteristics, then fit standard regression for inference.






5.1.4 Question 4: Random Forest Mechanics
In a random forest with 500 trees predicting healthcare costs from 12 variables:

How many variables would typically be considered at each split?
Why does considering only a subset of variables at each split improve the ensemble?
What is out-of-bag (OOB) error and why is it useful?







TipClick for Answers






m = 12/3 = 4 variables per split (default for regression is p/3).
Decorrelates the trees: If all trees considered all variables, they would all split on the same strongest predictor at the root, making them very similar. By randomly restricting the variables considered, different trees emphasize different predictors, making the ensemble more diverse. When we average diverse predictions, errors cancel out better than when averaging similar predictions.
OOB error: Each bootstrap sample includes only about 63% of observations. The remaining 37% are “out-of-bag” for that tree. We can predict these using the tree and compare to actual values. Averaging across all trees gives an error estimate without needing a separate test set. It’s useful because:

No need to set aside test data
More efficient use of training data
Unbiased estimate of test error

                      n_patients, replace = TRUE),

  icu_admission = sample(c("Yes", "No"), n_patients, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.15, 0.85)),

)

# Generate realistic LOS

  mutate(
    base_los = case_when(
      primary_dx == "Cardiac" ~ 4,
      primary_dx == "Respiratory" ~ 3.5,
      primary_dx == "GI" ~ 3,
      primary_dx == "Orthopedic" ~ 4.5,
      TRUE ~ 2.5

    age_effect = 0.02 * age,
    comorbidity_effect = 0.5 * n_comorbidities,
    surgery_effect = ifelse(surgery == "Yes", 2, 0),
    icu_effect = ifelse(icu_admission == "Yes", 3, 0),
    emergency_effect = ifelse(admission_type == "Emergency", 1.5, 0),

    expected_los = base_los + age_effect + comorbidity_effect +
                   surgery_effect + icu_effect + emergency_effect,

    los = round(pmax(1, expected_los + rnorm(n_patients, 0, 1.5)), 1)
  ) %>%

         surgery, icu_admission, los)

# Convert to factors

  mutate(across(c(sex, admission_type, primary_dx, surgery, icu_admission), as.factor))

text:
5.3 Case Study: Hospital Resource Utilization Prediction

5.3.1 Scenario
You are an analytics manager at a multi-hospital health system. The CFO has asked you to develop a model to predict annual healthcare resource utilization (measured as total RVUs - Relative Value Units) for patients in your accountable care organization. The goal is to:

Identify high-utilization patients for care management programs
Improve budget forecasting
Understand key drivers of resource utilization



5.3.2 Dataset


Show code
# Create RVU prediction dataset
set.seed(2024)
n_aco <- 1200

aco_data <- data.frame(
  patient_id = 1:n_aco,

  # Demographics
  age = round(runif(n_aco, 18, 89)),
  sex = sample(c("Male", "Female"), n_aco, replace = TRUE),

  # Clinical
  hcc_score = round(pmax(0.3, rnorm(n_aco, 1.2, 0.6)), 2),  # Risk score
  n_chronic = rpois(n_aco, 2),
  mental_health_dx = sample(c(0, 1), n_aco, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.7, 0.3)),

  # Access
  pcp_visits_prior = rpois(n_aco, 3),
  specialist_visits_prior = rpois(n_aco, 2),
  ed_visits_prior = rpois(n_aco, 0.5),

  # Social
  medicaid = sample(c(0, 1), n_aco, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.75, 0.25)),
  rural = sample(c(0, 1), n_aco, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.8, 0.2))
)

# Generate RVUs
aco_data <- aco_data %>%
  mutate(
    expected_rvu = 50 +
                   2 * age +
                   80 * hcc_score +
                   30 * n_chronic +
                   40 * mental_health_dx +
                   15 * pcp_visits_prior +
                   25 * specialist_visits_prior +
                   100 * ed_visits_prior +
                   30 * medicaid -
                   20 * rural +
                   # Interactions
                   3 * age * (hcc_score > 1.5) +
                   50 * mental_health_dx * (n_chronic > 2),

    annual_rvu = round(pmax(10, expected_rvu * exp(rnorm(n_aco, 0, 0.25))))
  ) %>%
  select(-expected_rvu)

# Convert to factors
aco_data <- aco_data %>%
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex),
    mental_health_dx = factor(mental_health_dx, labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    medicaid = factor(medicaid, labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    rural = factor(rural, labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  )

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
In ANOVA, the term “way” refers to the number of independent variables (or factors) we are examining:

One-Way ANOVA: Analyzes the effect of one factor on an outcome

Example: Does patient satisfaction differ across 4 hospital departments?
Factor: Department (4 levels: Emergency, Cardiology, Orthopedics, Oncology)
Outcome: Satisfaction score

Two-Way ANOVA: Analyzes the effects of two factors simultaneously on an outcome

Example: Does pain reduction depend on both treatment type AND disease severity?
Factor A: Treatment (2 levels: Standard, New)
Factor B: Severity (3 levels: Mild, Moderate, Severe)
Outcome: Pain reduction score






In healthcare settings, outcomes are rarely influenced by a single factor.
For example, the effectiveness of an intervention type (e.g., standard vs. intensive care) can vary depending on disease severity (e.g., mild, moderate, severe).
While one-way ANOVA can only examine one factor at a time, two-way ANOVA allows us to understand if the effect of one factor depends on the level of another factor. This is called an interaction effect, and it’s one of the most important concepts in healthcare research.
Two-way ANOVA allows us to:

Test the effect of Factor A (main effect of A, e.g., intervention type)
Test the effect of Factor B (main effect of B, e.g., disease severity)
Test whether the effect of A depends on B (interaction effect A × B, e.g., intervention type × disease severity)






A main effect is the overall effect of one factor, averaging across all levels of the other factor.

Main effect of Treatment: Does the treatment affect outcomes, regardless of patient group?
Main effect of Patient Group: Do patient groups differ in outcomes, regardless of treatment?




An interaction effect occurs when the effect of one factor depends on the level of another factor.

The new drug works well for younger patients but not for older patients
The training program improves performance for novice nurses (work experience < 2 years) but not experienced nurses (work experience > 2 years)

When an interaction is present, main effects can be misleading! If a drug helps one group but harms another, the “average” effect might be zero.

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Visualizing Interactions
The easiest way to understand interactions is through interaction plots, where we plot means for each combination of factors. The pattern of lines tells us about the interaction.

Pattern 1: Parallel Lines (No Interaction)
When there is no interaction, the effect of one factor is the same across all levels of the other factor. The lines in the interaction plot are parallel.









Interpretation: The new treatment improves outcomes by 15 points for both mild and severe patients. The treatment effect is consistent regardless of severity.


Pattern 2: Ordinal Interaction (Converging/Diverging Lines)
In an ordinal interaction, the lines converge or diverge but do not cross. The effect of one factor is larger at some levels of the other factor, but the direction is the same.









Interpretation: The new treatment helps both groups, but it helps severe patients much more (+25 points) than mild patients (+10 points). The treatment is beneficial for everyone, but especially for those with severe disease.


Pattern 3: Disordinal (Crossover) Interaction
In a disordinal (or crossover) interaction, the lines cross. The effect of one factor reverses direction at different levels of the other factor.









Interpretation: The new treatment helps severe patients (+30 points) but harms mild patients (-10 points). The main effect of treatment might appear small or non-significant because the positive and negative effects cancel out.

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Why Interactions Matter in Healthcare
Understanding interactions is important in healthcare management because:

Personalized medicine: Treatment effectiveness often varies by patient characteristics
Resource allocation: Interventions may work better in some settings or groups than others
Safety: A treatment safe for one population may be harmful for another
Policy decisions: Program effectiveness may depend on implementation context

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
What is it?
A two-way between-subjects ANOVA tests the effects of two independent variables (factors) on a continuous dependent variable, where different participants are in each combination of factor levels.

Key Components

Two factors (each with 2 or more levels)
Each participant is in only one cell of the design
Tests three effects: Main effect A, Main effect B, A × B interaction

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
When to Use It

Comparing the effectiveness of treatment types (e.g., medication A vs. B vs. C) across patient demographics (e.g., age groups, gender, comorbidity status)
Evaluating interventions (e.g., discharge planning programs: telehealth vs. in-person care) across facility types (e.g., academic medical centers, community hospitals, rural critical access hospitals)
Assessing programs (e.g., traditional lecture, simulation-based, blended learning) across staff experience levels (e.g., novice, intermediate, expert nurses)

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Scenario 1: Treatment × Disease Severity
Let’s think about the following case:
A clinical trial compares two treatments (Standard vs. Novel) for chronic pain across three severity levels (Mild, Moderate, Severe). The outcome is pain reduction score (0-100, higher = better).
Research on chronic pain management has shown that treatment effectiveness often varies by baseline disease severity and patient phenotype. Understanding these interactions is critical for personalized pain management approaches.
Research questions:

Does the novel treatment reduce pain more than standard care (main effect of treatment)?
Does pain reduction vary by baseline severity (the main effect of severity levels)?
Does the treatment effect depend on severity (interaction)?

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
The Formula
Two-way ANOVA partitions variance into four components:
\[SS_{total} = SS_A + SS_B + SS_{A \times B} + SS_{error}\]
Three F-statistics are calculated:
\[F_A = \frac{MS_A}{MS_{error}}, \quad F_B = \frac{MS_B}{MS_{error}}, \quad F_{A \times B} = \frac{MS_{A \times B}}{MS_{error}}\]
The degrees of freedom:

Factor A: \(df_A = a - 1\)
Factor B: \(df_B = b - 1\)
Interaction: \(df_{A \times B} = (a-1)(b-1)\)
Error: \(df_{error} = N - ab\)

Where

\(a\) = levels of A
\(b\) = levels of B
\(N\) = total sample size.

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Example: Treatment × Disease Severity
Let’s create a dataset and examine summary statistics.

# Pain reduction scores for 2 treatments × 3 severity levels
# 15 patients per cell = 90 total
n_per_cell <- 15

# Generate data with interaction effect
# Novel treatment works better for severe patients
set.seed(2026)

pain_data <- expand.grid(
  treatment = c("Standard", "Novel"),
  severity = c("Mild", "Moderate", "Severe"),
  subject = 1:n_per_cell
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Base effect of severity (less reduction for more severe)
    base = case_when(
      severity == "Mild" ~ 70,
      severity == "Moderate" ~ 55,
      severity == "Severe" ~ 40
    ),
    # Treatment effect varies by severity (interaction)
    treatment_effect = case_when(
      treatment == "Standard" ~ 0,
      treatment == "Novel" & severity == "Mild" ~ 5,
      treatment == "Novel" & severity == "Moderate" ~ 12,
      treatment == "Novel" & severity == "Severe" ~ 22
    ),
    # Add random error
    pain_reduction = base + treatment_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 6)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    severity = factor(severity, levels = c("Mild", "Moderate", "Severe")),
    treatment = factor(treatment, levels = c("Standard", "Novel"))
  )

Conducting Two-Way Between-Subjects ANOVA in R

anova_pain <- aov(pain_reduction ~ treatment * severity, data = pain_data)
summary(anova_pain)

treatment           1   5053    5053  140.65  < 2e-16 ***

treatment:severity  2   1011     505   14.06 5.39e-06 ***
Residuals          84   3018      36                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



Interpreting the ANOVA Table
The output shows three tests:

treatment: Main effect of treatment (averaging across severity levels)
severity: Main effect of severity (averaging across treatments)
treatment:severity: Interaction effect

Results interpretation:

Main effect of treatment: Significant main effect of treatment on average (pain reduction differs across treatments)
Main effect of severity: Significant main effect of severity (pain reduction differs across severity levels)
Interaction: Significant treatment X severity interaction (the treatment effect differs depending on severity level)



When Interaction is Significant

Do not interpret main effects in isolation when the interaction is significant!
The significant interaction tells us that the novel treatment’s benefit varies by severity. To understand this pattern, we need to examine simple effects.

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Simple Effects Analysis (post-hoc analysis)
Simple effects examine the effect of one factor at each level of the other factor. We use the emmeans package for this analysis.

# Get estimated marginal means
emm <- emmeans(anova_pain, ~ treatment | severity)

# Simple effects: treatment effect at each severity level
pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey")

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Example 2: Training Method × Experience Level
A hospital evaluates two training methods (Lecture vs. Simulation) for medication safety competency across three experience levels (Novice: <1 year, Intermediate: 1-5 years, Expert: >5 years).
Research comparing training approaches has demonstrated that simulation-based education is particularly effective for novice nurses, while the benefits may vary by experience level.
Let’s create a dataset.

# Generate data with crossover interaction
n_cell <- 12

training_data <- expand.grid(
  method = c("Lecture", "Simulation"),
  experience = c("Novice", "Intermediate", "Expert"),
  subject = 1:n_cell
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Crossover interaction: simulation helps novices but lecture helps experts
    score = case_when(
      method == "Lecture" & experience == "Novice" ~ 68,
      method == "Lecture" & experience == "Intermediate" ~ 78,
      method == "Lecture" & experience == "Expert" ~ 88,
      method == "Simulation" & experience == "Novice" ~ 82,
      method == "Simulation" & experience == "Intermediate" ~ 80,
      method == "Simulation" & experience == "Expert" ~ 79
    ) + rnorm(n(), 0, 4),
    experience = factor(experience, levels = c("Novice", "Intermediate", "Expert"))
  )











# Two-way ANOVA
anova_training <- aov(score ~ method * experience, data = training_data)

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Practice Activity 1: Intervention × Facility Type
A health system evaluates the effect of care transition program on readmission rates (30-days readmission rate in %) across facility types. Analyze whether the intervention effect depends on facility type.
Care Transition Programs help patients move safely from hospital to home, reducing probability of readmission:

Standard Discharge: Basic discharge instructions, prescription reconciliation, follow-up appointment scheduled
Enhanced Transition Program: Includes all standard elements + dedicated transition coordinator, post-discharge phone call within 48 hours, home medication review, connection to community resources

Facility Types differ in resources, patient populations, and care complexity:

Urban Academic Medical Centers: Large teaching hospitals treating complex cases, with many specialists, electronic health systems, and dedicated staff for care coordination
Suburban Community Hospitals: Mid-sized hospitals serving local communities with standard medical services and moderate staffing levels
Rural Critical Access Hospitals: Small hospitals (<25 beds) in remote areas with limited specialists and support staff; patients often travel long distances for care

Studies have found that enhanced transition programs reduce readmissions more effectively in some settings than others. Academic medical centers, which already have baseline infrastructure and care coordinators, may see smaller improvements from adding enhanced programs compared to their standard discharge processes. In contrast, rural hospitals, which often lack dedicated transition staff, may experience larger reductions in readmissions when enhanced programs are implemented, despite having fewer overall resources. Community hospitals typically fall between these two extremes. These differences suggest that “one-size-fits-all” transition programs may not be the most cost-effective approach across diverse facility types.

# 30-day readmission rates (%)
n_cell <- 10
set.seed(2006)

intervention_data <- expand.grid(
  program = c("Standard Discharge", "Enhanced Transition"),
  facility = c("Urban Academic", "Suburban Community", "Rural Critical Access"),
  id = 1:n_cell
) %>%
  mutate(
    readmit_rate = case_when(
      program == "Standard Discharge" & facility == "Urban Academic" ~ 14,
      program == "Standard Discharge" & facility == "Suburban Community" ~ 12,
      program == "Standard Discharge" & facility == "Rural Critical Access" ~ 16,
      program == "Enhanced Transition" & facility == "Urban Academic" ~ 13,
      program == "Enhanced Transition" & facility == "Suburban Community" ~ 9,
      program == "Enhanced Transition" & facility == "Rural Critical Access" ~ 8
    ) + rnorm(n(), 0, 1.5)
  )

# Your code here:
# 1. Create an interaction plot
# 2. Run two-way ANOVA
# 3. Conduct simple effects analysis if interaction is significant
# 4. Interpret the results for healthcare administrators



Code
# Solution
anova_int <- aov(readmit_rate ~ program * facility, data = intervention_data)
summary(anova_int)
emmeans(anova_int, ~ program | facility) %>% pairs(adjust = "tukey")

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Practice Activity 2: Medication × Age Group
A healthcare system compares the effectiveness of two pain medications across three age groups to inform formulary decisions and prescribing guidelines.
Context:
Pain Medications represent different treatment options:

Drug A: Standard anti-inflammatory medication
Drug B: Combination medication targeting multiple pain pathways

Age Groups differ in how their bodies process medications and respond to treatment:

Young Adults (18-40): Bodies process drugs quickly, generally have fewer other health conditions
Middle-Aged (41-65): Bodies process drugs more slowly than younger adults, more likely to have conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes
Older Adults (65+): Bodies process drugs most slowly, often take multiple medications, higher risk of drug side effects and interactions

Outcome Variable: Pain relief score (0-100 scale, higher scores = better pain control)
What Research Has Shown:
Clinical studies have found that combination pain medications (Drug B) may work differently across age groups. In younger patients, combination drugs often provide only modest improvements over standard medications, possibly because their bodies process drugs efficiently regardless of the drug type. However, in older patients, combination medications that work through multiple pathways have shown significantly better pain relief compared to standard single-mechanism drugs. This may be because older adults’ bodies respond better when pain is targeted from multiple angles simultaneously. Middle-aged patients typically show intermediate responses. Understanding these age-related patterns helps hospitals make evidence-based decisions about which medications to stock and prescribe for different patient populations.

n_cell <- 15

medication_data <- expand.grid(
  medication = c("Drug A", "Drug B"),
  age_group = c("Young (18-40)", "Middle (41-65)", "Older (65+)"),
  patient = 1:n_cell
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Ordinal interaction
    pain_relief = case_when(
      medication == "Drug A" ~ 55 + rnorm(n(), 0, 6),
      medication == "Drug B" & age_group == "Young (18-40)" ~ 58 + rnorm(n(), 0, 6),
      medication == "Drug B" & age_group == "Middle (41-65)" ~ 68 + rnorm(n(), 0, 6),
      medication == "Drug B" & age_group == "Older (65+)" ~ 78 + rnorm(n(), 0, 6)
    )
  )

# Your code here:



Code
# Solution
anova_med <- aov(pain_relief ~ medication * age_group, data = medication_data)
summary(anova_med)
emmeans(anova_med, ~ medication | age_group) %>% pairs(adjust = "tukey")

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
What is it?
A two-way within-subjects ANOVA (also called two-way repeated-measures ANOVA) tests the effects of two factors where the same participants experience all combinations of both factors.

Key Characteristics

Same participants measured under all conditions
Both factors are within-subjects (repeated measures)
More powerful than between-subjects designs (controls for individual differences)
Requires fewer participants

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
When to Use It
Use two-way within-subjects ANOVA when the same participants are measured under all combinations of two factors:

Same patients tested with different medications (e.g., Drug A, Drug B, Drug C) at different times of day (e.g., morning, evening)
Same staff evaluated on multiple tasks (e.g., vital signs, medication administration, charting) across multiple assessment periods (e.g., pre-training, post-training, 3-month follow-up)
Same clinics measured on different metrics (e.g., patient satisfaction, wait time, quality scores) in different seasons (e.g., winter, spring, summer, fall)

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
section: Scenario: Medication Type × Time of Day
text:
Scenario: Medication Type × Time of Day
A clinical study examines whether medication effectiveness varies by time of administration. The same 20 patients receive each of three medications at two different times (morning and evening), with appropriate rest periods between medications.
Study Design:
This is a within-subjects design where each patient tries all medication and time combinations:

Each patient receives Med A in the morning, Med A in the evening
Each patient receives Med B in the morning, Med B in the evening
Each patient receives Med C in the morning, Med C in the evening
Total: 6 conditions per patient (3 medications × 2 times)
Rest periods (washout periods) are included between medications to ensure one drug doesn’t affect the next

Medications Being Tested:

Med A: Standard pain reliever
Med B: Extended-release pain medication
Med C: Fast-acting pain medication

Outcome Variable: Medication effectiveness score (0-100, higher = better pain control)
Research has found that medication timing can significantly affect pain relief. Studies show that some pain medications work better when taken in the evening, providing longer pain relief with fewer side effects, while others may be more effective in the morning. Understanding these timing patterns helps doctors make better prescribing recommendations, potentially improving patient outcomes without increasing medication doses.
Let’s create a dataset

# Same 20 patients, all conditions
set.seed(2026)
n_patients <- 20

# Generate data
within_data <- expand.grid(
  patient_id = 1:n_patients,
  medication = c("Med A", "Med B", "Med C"),
  time = c("Morning", "Evening")
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Patient random effect
    patient_effect = rep(rnorm(n_patients, 0, 5), 6),
    # Fixed effects with interaction
    # Med A (standard): works better in evening (like NSAIDs in research)
    # Med B (extended-release): similar effectiveness both times
    # Med C (fast-acting): works better in morning when body is active
    fixed = case_when(
      medication == "Med A" & time == "Morning" ~ 63,
      medication == "Med A" & time == "Evening" ~ 72,
      medication == "Med B" & time == "Morning" ~ 70,
      medication == "Med B" & time == "Evening" ~ 71,
      medication == "Med C" & time == "Morning" ~ 77,
      medication == "Med C" & time == "Evening" ~ 65
    ),
    effectiveness = fixed + patient_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 3)
  )

# Two-way within-subjects ANOVA

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
section: Practice Activity 3: Task Type × Shift Period
text:
Practice Activity 3: Task Type × Shift Period
A hospital nursing director evaluates whether nurse performance on different task types changes throughout a shift. The same 15 nurses are evaluated on two task types across three shift periods.
Study Design:
This is a within-subjects design where each nurse is evaluated under all task-period combinations:

Each nurse performs documentation tasks at the beginning, middle, and end of shift
Each nurse performs patient care tasks at the beginning, middle, and end of shift
Total: 6 evaluations per nurse (2 task types × 3 shift periods)

Task Types:

Documentation: Completing patient charts, entering data into electronic health records, processing admission/discharge paperwork
Patient Care: Direct patient interactions including vital signs monitoring, medication administration, patient education, responding to patient needs

Shift Periods:

Beginning: First 2-3 hours of 12-hour shift (nurses are fresh but orientation to patients is ongoing)
Middle: Hours 4-8 of shift (nurses are familiar with patients, workload is often highest)
End: Final 2-3 hours of shift (fatigue may set in, handoff preparation begins)

Outcome Variable: Performance score (0-100, based on supervisor observation, higher = better performance)
Understanding how different tasks are affected by shift fatigue helps hospital administrators make evidence-based staffing and workflow decisions. For example, if documentation quality declines significantly toward the end of shifts while patient care remains stable, managers might schedule additional clerical support during late shift hours or redesign workflows to complete complex documentation earlier in shifts. This can improve both staff well-being and patient safety.

n_nurses <- 15

task_data <- expand.grid(
  nurse_id = 1:n_nurses,
  task = c("Documentation", "Patient Care"),
  period = c("Beginning", "Middle", "End")
) %>%
  mutate(
    nurse_effect = rep(rnorm(n_nurses, 0, 4), 6),
    # Performance declines more for documentation than patient care
    fixed = case_when(
      task == "Documentation" & period == "Beginning" ~ 90,
      task == "Documentation" & period == "Middle" ~ 82,
      task == "Documentation" & period == "End" ~ 70,
      task == "Patient Care" & period == "Beginning" ~ 88,
      task == "Patient Care" & period == "Middle" ~ 85,
      task == "Patient Care" & period == "End" ~ 80
    ),
    performance = fixed + nurse_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 3),
    period = factor(period, levels = c("Beginning", "Middle", "End"))
  )

# Your code here:
# 1. Create interaction plot
# 2. Run two-way within-subjects ANOVA
# 3. Interpret the interaction



Code
# Solution
task_anova <- aov(performance ~ task * period + Error(nurse_id/(task * period)),
                  data = task_data)
summary(task_anova)
emmeans(task_anova, ~ task | period) %>% pairs(adjust = "tukey")

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
What is it?
A mixed design ANOVA combines both between-subjects and within-subjects factors. This is one of the most common designs in healthcare research.

Key Characteristics

One or more between-subjects factors: Different participants in each group
One or more within-subjects factors: Same participants measured repeatedly
Tests main effects of both factor types and their interaction

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
When to Use It
Use mixed design ANOVA when different groups of participants are measured repeatedly over time:

Clinical trials: Treatment group (e.g., new drug, standard drug, placebo) × Time points (e.g., baseline, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months)
Training studies: Program type (e.g., online learning, in-person workshop, blended approach) × Assessment occasions (e.g., before training, immediately after, 1-month follow-up, 3-month follow-up)
Quality improvement: Intervention group (e.g., standard care, enhanced protocol) × Measurement periods (e.g., before intervention, 3 months after, 6 months after, 12 months after)

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Scenario: Training Program × Assessment Time
Let’s think about the following case:
A hospital compares three training programs for improving nursing competency. Nurses are randomly assigned to one program (between-subjects factor) and assessed at three time points (within-subjects factor): Before training, Immediately after training, and 3 months later.
Study Design:
This is a mixed design where different nurses are assigned to different programs (between-subjects), but each nurse is tested multiple times (within-subjects):

60 nurses total (20 assigned to each program)
Each nurse is tested 3 times: before training, right after training, 3 months later
The question: Do different training programs show different patterns of learning and retention over time?

Training Programs:

Traditional Lecture: Classroom instruction with PowerPoint presentations, lectures, and written materials. Lower cost, can train many nurses at once.
Simulation-Based: Hands-on practice with medical mannequins and equipment in a simulated hospital environment. Higher cost, smaller class sizes, allows practicing skills safely.
Blended Learning: Combination of online modules for theory (completed at own pace) plus in-person skill practice sessions. Moderate cost, flexible scheduling.

Outcome Variable: Competency test score (0-100, covering both knowledge and skills, higher scores = higher competencies)
Studies comparing nursing training methods have found that simulation-based and blended learning approaches generally produce better learning outcomes than traditional lecture-only methods, with students scoring higher on competency tests. However, the key management question is about long-term retention: Do more expensive training methods maintain their advantage over time, or do all methods “fade” equally? Research shows that hands-on training methods (simulation and blended) show better long-term retention compared to lecture-only approaches. Understanding these patterns helps hospitals justify the higher upfront costs of simulation or blended programs if they provide lasting benefits.

n_per_group <- 20

mixed_data <- expand.grid(
  nurse_id = 1:(n_per_group * 3),
  time = c("Pre", "Post", "3 Months")
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Assign to groups
    program = rep(rep(c("Traditional", "Simulation", "Blended"),
                      each = n_per_group), 3),
    # Nurse random effect
    nurse_effect = rep(rnorm(n_per_group * 3, 0, 4), 3),
    # Fixed effects
    fixed = case_when(
      # Traditional: modest improvement, significant decay
      program == "Traditional" & time == "Pre" ~ 65,
      program == "Traditional" & time == "Post" ~ 75,
      program == "Traditional" & time == "3 Months" ~ 66,
      # Simulation: good improvement, well maintained
      program == "Simulation" & time == "Pre" ~ 65,
      program == "Simulation" & time == "Post" ~ 84,
      program == "Simulation" & time == "3 Months" ~ 79,
      # Blended: best improvement, well maintained
      program == "Blended" & time == "Pre" ~ 65,
      program == "Blended" & time == "Post" ~ 88,
      program == "Blended" & time == "3 Months" ~ 85
    ),
    score = fixed + nurse_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 3),
    time = factor(time, levels = c("Pre", "Post", "3 Months"))
